The targets in terms of quantity of fuel saved are not contained in the project prodoc. I have taken the liberty of making a small estimate.
A household can consume around 1 to 2 kg of charcoal and/or 5 kg of wood per day. Assuming that half of the planned cooking stoves are wood-burning and the other half charcoal-burning, and assuming an energy efficiency of 50 percent, we get this result. The amount of fuel avoided is 3250 g per day, including 750 g of charcoal.

(Ardhi's estimate)
Average charcoal's calorific value 30 MJ/kg
Average wood's CV = 18.5/kg

Energy saved per day  = (30*2500 + 18.5*750)/1000 = 88,\.875 MJ
Energy saved per year = 88,875*365 = 32,439.375

Joining force with six partners joining to implement SHIFT project, UNDP is responsible for the design and implementation of two work packages. The project aims to reduce the operational costs of education and public facilities in East Jerusalem through investments in renewable energy, primarily solar systems installed on rooftops and in external yards, with an estimated capacity of 1.6 MWp, in addition to investments in energy efficiency.

Such investments will generate clean energy while also contributing to decreasing electricity expenses of schools and local CSO’s.

Consequently, this will be generating savings, which in turn can be utilized for maintenance, covering operational expenses, quality education and development purposes. Some of facilities will be benefited from energy efficiency activities, to reduce the electricity consumption, as well as upgrading electricity networks and installations.

Investments in solar energy will also raise students’, educators’ and communities’ awareness about promoting renewable energy, mitigating climate change, reducing carbon emissions (carbon footprint) and protecting the environment at large.

Overall, the project intends to support the transition of East Jerusalem schools’ and selected public institutions towards green and renewable energy, which can also significantly contribute to and strengthen schools’ and local systems resilience and self-reliance.

The project will target 20 schools, 3 hospitals and 7 public facilities.

column3: Water Energy Food (WEF) Nexus in the West Bank
column11: MW
column14:
The Water-Energy-Food (WEF) Nexus project responds directly to several pressing challenges faced by communities in the West Bank. The region experiences chronic water scarcity due to limited natural resources, growing population demands, and the effects of climate change, which together place immense pressure on existing water infrastructure. Furthermore, the high cost and unreliable supply of conventional energy further complicate the delivery of water services. These intertwined issues threaten food security, limit economic opportunities, and hinder community resilience.
To address these obstacles, the project will introduce solar-powered water wells ( in the design stage to target 27 water facility , In implementation stage under the avilable resources : 15 water facilitites to be targeted, generating 1800 Kwp) , leveraging renewable energy to ensure more reliable and sustainable water supply. By integrating solar technology and energy-efficient systems, the initiative seeks to reduce operational costs, lower dependencies on fossil fuels, and enhance the resilience of water facilities throughout the West Bank.
Beyond infrastructure upgrades, the project is committed to strengthening the institutional and technical capacities of the Palestinian Water Authority (PWA), the National Water Company/West Bank Water Department (NWC/WBWD), and the Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority (PENRA). This capacity building includes technical training, the creation of a Resilience Fund for sustainable investment, and improved operational procedures.
By embracing innovative technology, building local expertise, and fostering cooperative management of resources, the WEF Nexus project aspires to deliver long-lasting improvements in water access, energy efficiency, and agricultural productivity—ultimately enhancing the well-being and resilience of communities across the West Bank.

column11: Investment projects in low carbon energy ($)
column14:
The GTALCC Project facilitated 4 investment projects in low carbon energy. 3 were completed but the solar PV project with the city of Putrajaya was cancelled due to the regulatory requirement on the installation site.

1. Collaboration with the city of Putrajaya on Proof of Concept (POC) to determine Solar PV’s technical and commercial viability for government buildings with alternative solutions to increase adoption of renewable energy. The demonstration at Putrajaya’s Precinct 4 parking complex will not commence as it does not meet the authority requirement for Net Energy Metering (NEM) Scheme and high financial investment for installation of Solar PV and infrastructure works for Self-Consumption (SELCO) scheme.

2. Collaboration with the city of Petaling Jaya - Business proposal development is on-going to identify package deals to lower costs for users and increase uptake in the city. The project shall support Petaling Jaya on the promotion of the packages once ready. An EPC Partner shall be selected to be MBPJ’s Promotional and Implementation Partner for the Solar PV Bundle Purchase Scheme Initiative and shall be able to provide competitive Solar PV Bundle Packages to design, fabricate, supply, install, test and commission Solar PV onto rooftops, for a minimum of 50 houses. 

3. Collaboration with Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) Corporation - Solar PV installation of 37kWp will be installed at Taman Midah MRT Station Park and Ride Building.

4. Installation of Building Energy Monitoring Systems completed in March 2020 for Hang Tuah Jaya Municipal Council (MPHTJ) in collaboration with Sustainable Energy Development Authority (SEDA) Malaysia.

column3: GTALCC
column11: Investment projects in low carbon transportation ($)
column14:
A total of 4 investment projects in low carbon transportation facilitated by the GTALCC project already completed and 3 more are in progress.

1. International Peer Reviewer engaged by the project provided technical assistance in 2020 with recommendations on the preliminary design to achieve Bus Rapid Transport (BRT) Gold Standard. Some of the recommendations were adopted into the design by the BRT Lead Consultant and Iskandar Malaysia BRT (IMBRT) team.  

2. The IMBRT technology pilot is on-going since March 2021 with various bus technologies on trial in Johor Bahru.

3. The B100 (Bio-Fuel) for Public Transportation – RapidBus Kuala Lumpur / Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) Corporation is in the final stages of pilot programme, pending procurement of a specialised mobile fueling system. It is targeted to commence in Q2 2022.

4. The design study for on-road bike lane between Putrajaya Sentral and the government complex is being finalized. It will identify the best route for a dedicated bike lane. The technical studies supported by the project on Road Safety Audit (RSA) 2 and 3 have been completed and this shall provide inputs to the designing of a safe bike lane on existing road.

5. The pilot project has installed 10 units of EV chargers at 6 locations i.e. Petaling Jaya (4 units at 2 locations), Shah Alam (3 units at 2 locations), and Kuala Lumpur (3 units at 2 locations). The final report provides a guideline for apartments and building owners on type of installations that can be carried out, the procedures, and potential business models.

6. The electric bicycles are being used by Enforcement and Maintenance staff members of Putrajaya Corporation in Putrajaya and Sepang Municipal Council in Cyberjaya.

7. The Bicycle Access Ramps installed at the stairways of 2 bridges in Putrajaya is now part of the city’s comprehensive cycle network.
